title: $6 million for research on climate and mental health
text: Media event date: 24 September 2026 Date published: 24 September 2026 Media type: Media release Audience: General public The Albanese Government is committed to addressing the human health impacts of climate change, with $6 million for Australia’s leading researchers to study and combat the mental health challenges of climate change. The Australian Government has awarded $6 million to 3 new research projects through the Medical Research Future Fund. Projects will study and devise methods to improve the mental health and wellbeing of people affected by climate change, with a particular focus on First Nations people. Adelaide University, the University of Melbourne and the Menzies School of Health Research have each been awarded almost $2 million each to research, advise on policy, and implement local community strategies. Each of these projects was identified through a competitive application process, and assessed by independent assessment committees. Climate change disproportionately affects First Nations communities as the distress of unprecedented droughts, longer summers and continued extreme weather events lead to heritage and environmental loss. Two of the three projects will include a focus on the experience of First Nations communities. Full details of the awarded grants are in the table below. Quotes attributable to Assistant Minister White: “The grants from the Albanese Government will provide some of Australia’s top researchers with the funds they need to improve mental health support for Australian’s impacted by climate change. “These projects will deliver a range of practical, community-led responses to emerging mental health challenges with an important focus on First Nations communities impacted by climate change.” Quotes attributable to Assistant Minister McBride: “Two in five young people experience mental health challenges each year. These aren’t just numbers - they’re our family, our friends, our teammates and our colleagues. “We’re living through challenging times, and supporting the mental health of Australians remains a clear priority for the Albanese Labor Government. “If you’re feeling overwhelmed, I encourage you to speak with a health professional at your local Medicare Mental Health Centre or reach out to headspace.” Applicant name Organisation Project Title Project Description Grant Value (GST exclusive) Associate Professor Toby Freeman Adelaide University Helping prevent mental health deterioration at scale: Mitigating the population mental health impacts from climate breakdown-related loss or anticipated loss of heritage As climate breakdown intensifies, communities are increasingly experiencing psychological distress. In particular, the loss or anticipated loss of natural and cultural heritage, including cherished landscapes, ecosystems, and culturally significant places, can lead to grief, distress and anxiety. This project will deliver practical resources for communities and the mental health system, and actionable policy recommendations to mitigate mental health impacts of heritage and environmental loss. $1,942,278.00 Associate Professor Supriya Mathew Menzies School of Health Research Pintupi-led climate yarning to mitigate climate change-related mental health risks In partnership with Pintupi people and the Pintupi Homelands Health Service, the project will co-design, implement, and evaluate strategies and resources aimed at reducing both current and emerging mental health risks linked to climate-related stress. By working closely with the community and local stakeholders, the project will empower residents and remote health staff to take an active role in addressing the social and emotional wellbeing challenges brought on by climate change. $1,997,077.60 Professor Victoria Palmer University of Melbourne Gathering the parts, making the whole: Lost but not Forgotten, participatory ecosystems to mitigate impacts of climate change on mental health Climate changes disproportionately impact Indigenous communities, and younger generations are expressing increased eco-grief and eco-anxieties. Across 50 remote art and cultural centres, communities of the Great Southern region of WA, Tennant Creek in NT and a national story sharing project, we will illustrate how participatory ecosystems protect culture, Country and offer two-way learning to mitigate the mental health impacts of climate change and co-design prevention for future generations. $1,994,458.10 Total Commitment Expenditure (GST exclusive) $5,933,813.70 Minister: The Hon Rebecca White MP The Hon Emma McBride MP Tags: Mental health and suicide prevention

title: Migrant women to discuss health in their language
text: Media event date: 23 September 2026 Date published: 23 September 2026 Media type: Media release Audience: General public The Australian Government is continuing its national program to provide health information and support to migrant and refugee women in their own languages. Through a $10.8 million investment over 2 years, the Multicultural Centre for Women's Health will continue leading the Health in My Language Program in partnership with 7 organisations across the country. Migrant and refugee women can face significant barriers to accessing health information and services, including language differences, lower health literacy and challenges navigating an unfamiliar healthcare system. The Health in My Language Program helps address these barriers by training and supporting bilingual health educators to deliver free, culturally safe health education sessions in participants’ preferred language. Using shared language, evidence-based and up-to-date knowledge, lived experience and strong community connections, educators support women to navigate services and make informed decisions about their health and wellbeing. The sessions provide a safe and supportive environment where women can ask questions, share experiences and build confidence in managing their own health and the health of their families. Since commencing in 2022, the Government has invested around $35 million in the program. More than 8,000 people from migrant and refugee communities across every state and territory have participated in sessions delivered in more than 30 different languages. The investment will continue to address a critical gap in culturally responsive health information and help ensure more women have the information, support and confidence to access services they need. Quotes attributable to the Minister for Multicultural Affairs, Dr Anne Aly: "Language should never be a barrier to accessing important health information, support and services. “This program ensures migrant and refugee women can receive trusted, culturally appropriate information in a language they understand. "By empowering women with knowledge and confidence, the Health in My Language Program is strengthening the health and wellbeing of individuals, families and communities across Australia." Quotes attributable to Assistant Minister White: "Good health starts with having information that is accessible, relevant and delivered in a way that resonates with people’s experience. "What makes this program so effective is that it is delivered by trusted bilingual health educators who understand the communities they work with and create safe spaces for women to ask questions, share experiences and learn from one another. "The evaluation shows these sessions are making a real difference. Women are building confidence, better understanding their health needs and feeling more empowered to navigate the healthcare system. "When women feel informed and supported, the benefits extend far beyond the individual to families. and communities and future generations." Quotes attributable to case studies of women attending Health in My Language sessions: Case study 1 : “Before I started the HIML sessions, I was anxious and overwhelmed whenever I thought about using the healthcare system. I had never attended any health education programs before and due to language barriers… I had no idea how to ask for help or navigate the health system… It left me feeling unsure, isolated, and disconnected from taking care of my health. Today, I feel much more comfortable and confident when using health services. The knowledge I gained gave me the courage to overcome my past hesitations and encouraged me to go to the clinic” Case study 2: “About a year ago, I attended a Health in My Language session about women’s health and cancer awareness. During that session, information about stomach and bowel cancer especially stayed with me. At the time, I remember feeling worried because some of the symptoms discussed sounded familiar to me…After the session ended, I approached the health educator privately and shared my concerns. For the first time, I openly spoke about the symptoms that had been worrying me for a long time. The educator listened carefully, without judgment, and helped me book an appointment with a GP. At the medical appointment, I explained my symptoms and concerns. Even though routine screening was not yet recommended for my age, the doctor decided to organise further medical investigations because of the symptoms I described. After completing the tests, doctors identified changes that required medical attention and early treatment. I was told that addressing the issue early helped prevent more serious complications and possible long-term consequences.” Minister: The Hon Rebecca White MP Tags: Women's health

title: Stronger NDIS integrity controls save billions
text: Media event date: 23 September 2026 Date published: 23 September 2026 Media type: Media release Audience: General public Stronger NDIS integrity systems put in place by the Australian Government have delivered $2.1 billion in savings and benefits through stopping non-compliant payments and protecting participant funding from misuse. Between November 2022 and June 2026, integrity interventions have prevented $1.2 billion in fraudulent and non-compliant payments, while $900 million in participant funding was redirected away from bad actors and towards legitimate supports and services. The ongoing impacts of integrity interventions implemented by 30 June 2026 are expected to deliver a further $2 billion in savings and benefits by 30 June 2029, taking the total to $4.1 billion. These benefits are expected to increase as future interventions are implemented. The Albanese Government has invested over $1.35 billion in tackling fraud and non-compliance in the NDIS, including over $800 million in this year’s budget. These investments have enabled the NDIA to embed fraud detection and prevention controls in NDIS systems, moving to a system that identifies and stops suspicious payments before money leaves a participant’s plan. The NDIA assesses over 700,000 claims a day with strengthened controls designed to make it easier to get claiming right and harder for fraud, non-compliance and misuse to occur. It uses interventions to protect participants such as manual payment reviews and pre-payment checks of individual claims that have been identified as potentially high risk. Over the past 2 financial years, more than 265,000 high-risk claims worth more than $420 million were reviewed before payment with over 135,000 of these claims rejected. This stopped more than $255 million worth of suspicious claims from leaving participants’ plans. In the last financial year, 75% of high-risk entities subject to manual payment reviews stopped claiming against participants’ plans within 6 months. The Fraud Fusion Taskforce has disrupted over 5,900 providers identified as high risk or associated with incorrect or non-compliant claiming practices. In the 12 months prior to disruption, these providers claimed approximately $1.1 billion from the NDIS and over $6.5 billion since the scheme commenced. The NDIA regularly makes referrals to its Fraud Fusion Taskforce partners, including for criminal investigation, following a manual payment review. Another major upgrade is the NDIS Integrity Portal launched in June 2026, the agency’s first dedicated online channel for collecting and scrutinising evidence for claims before payment. Early results have been strong, with 2,500 claims worth almost $1 million reviewed and 1,794 claims worth $656,000 rejected. The Integrity Portal lays the foundation for broader digital evidence assessment across NDIS systems including a new provider enrolment and digital payments system in development as part of the next phase of the Crack Down on Fraud program. The NDIA began building the Digital Enrolment, Access and Payment Program in July 2026 with full rollout expected by June 2030. The new system will further strengthen claims and payment controls while improving the experience for participants and providers. These system improvements are backed by stronger laws. The NDIS Amendment (Securing the NDIS for Future Generations) Act 2026 , passed by Parliament in August 2026, further strengthens the integrity framework through new civil penalties and expanded monitoring and investigation powers. The NDIS Amendment (Integrity and Safeguarding) Act 2025 , passed in April 2026, modernises NDIS claims through mandated electronic claim forms and gives the NDIA legal powers to request evidence before claims are paid. Quotes attributable to Senator Jenny McAllister, Minister for the NDIS: “This is what placing integrity into the design of the NDIS’s framework looks like. “We do these things because we believe in integrity for its own sake. To protect public finances. To make sure funds don’t end up supporting criminal syndicates. “But more importantly, we do this because we want the scheme to deliver for the people who need it.” Minister: Senator the Hon Jenny McAllister Tags: Disability and carers

title: Mollymook set to become more accessible for people with disability
text: Media event date: 22 September 2026 Date published: 22 September 2026 Media type: Media release Audience: General public Mollymook beach will be one of the 11 beaches, play spaces and national parks across NSW that will become easier for people with disability to enjoy. Four new beach wheelchairs, available for use and stored at Mollymook Surf Life Saving Club, will give locals and visitors greater independence to enjoy the beach. This joint investment from the Shoalhaven City Council and Albanese Government builds on existing accessibility features at Mollymook Beach, including accessible toilets and playground facilities, and beach-wheelchair hire. The new wheelchairs are part of the latest round of funding under the Accessible Australia initiative, which will provide $3.8 million for 37 new inclusive amenities projects across Victoria, the Northern Territory, Tasmania, South Australia, NSW, the ACT and Western Australia. This includes $1.1 million for 11 projects in NSW, funded by the Albanese Government and administered by the Minns Government. For the first time the Accessible Australia initiative is delivering beach wheelchairs, floating wheelchairs and beach matting, with eight inclusive beach projects, 12 fixed Changing Places facilities, five portable Changing Places facilities and 12 inclusive play spaces nationwide. Funding is delivered through Federation Funding Agreement Schedules with the government working in partnership with participating states and territories. Most of the facilities are expected to be completed by mid‑2028. Quotes attributable to Senator McAllister, Federal Minister for the NDIS: “There’s nothing more Australian than a day at the beach. We want everyone to be able to enjoy it. “These new beach wheelchairs will make it easier for people with disability to enjoy the much-loved Mollymook Beach with their family and friends. “I’m proud to be part of a government that invests in infrastructure and amenities to make sure people living with disability can enjoy our natural environment.” Quotes attributable to Fiona Phillips, Federal Member for Gilmore: “Mollymook is a family favourite with locals and visitors alike, and having disability access to the beach is so important in such a popular tourist destination. “With the fantastic Livvi’s Place inclusive playground right next door, it means families can come and make the most of a range of accessible facilities at Mollymook Beach. “Salt water, sunshine and fresh air can be so rejuvenating for the mind and body, so I’m really excited that these wheelchairs will allow everyone to enjoy the waves. “I’m sure they will bring huge smiles to the faces of many children and adults with disabilities – especially when the local dolphins come and say hello.” Quotes attributable to Kate Washington, State Minister for Disability Inclusion: "Independence and dignity don't stop at the water's edge and these new beach wheelchairs at Mollymook will be a gamechanger for locals with disability. "This is a practical but significant investment brought together by all levels of government working to make our communities fairer and more inclusive.” Quotes attributable to Liza Butler, State Member for South Coast: “We are incredibly lucky to have one of the most beautiful coastlines in Australia, and I’m thrilled that more locals and visitors with disability will now be able to enjoy everything Mollymook Beach has to offer. “I’m proud to see all levels of government working together to make one of our most loved beaches more accessible and inclusive, ensuring more people can experience the sand, surf and beauty of Mollymook as the warmer weather arrives.” Quotes attributable to Shoalhaven Mayor Patricia White: “We welcome the awarding of more than $22,000 to Shoalhaven City Council in the form of an Accessible Australia grant. “We’re thrilled to receive this Federal Government funding, arranged through the NSW Government. This generous grant has enabled Council to purchase four new all-terrain beach wheelchairs to be housed at Mollymook Surf Life Saving Club. There’s growing community demand for these important assets and they will be widely used by local people with a disability to access the water at stunning Mollymook Beach. “Two of the beach wheelchairs are suitable for adults and two can be used by children or smaller adults. They will be available to loan at no charge from Saturday 26 September. It brings the number of beach wheelchairs available for use at Mollymook to six, and there’s now 17 in total across the Shoalhaven. The latest additions strengthen Council’s ability to improve access and inclusion for people with disability. We want to ensure that all people have fair and equitable access to the services and activities that our region has to offer.” Minister: Senator the Hon Jenny McAllister Tags: Disability and carers

title: PBS listing to benefit over 100,000 Australians with eczema
text: Media event date: 18 September 2026 Date published: 18 September 2026 Media type: Media release Audience: General public The Australian Government’s continuing investment in cheaper medicines means more than 100,000 Australians with eczema will benefit from a new treatment being listed on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS). From October 1, Tacrolimus0.1% ointment, marketed as aZematop will be listed on the PBS for eligible patients aged 16 years and over with moderate to severe atopic dermatitis, also known as eczema. Eczema is a chronic skin condition that causes dry, itchy, painful and inflamed skin. The condition can be relapsing and remitting, with periods when symptoms become worse, known as flares. Symptoms can significantly affect a person’s quality of life. The treatment will be for people aged 16 years and over with moderate to severe atopic dermatitis. More than 143,000 Australians are expected to benefit from the listing each year. Without PBS subsidy, patients could pay more than $54 per script. In addition, from 1 October, more than 5,700 Australians with severe asthma or hives are expected to benefit from new pre-filled pen forms of Omalizumab (Omlyclo ® ) which would cost more than $450 per script without the PBS subsidy. Eligible patients will instead pay a maximum of $25 per script, or $7.70 with a concession card. Since July 2022, the Albanese Government has approved extra funding for 497 new and amended listings on the PBS. Quotes attributable to Minister Butler: “The Albanese Government is committed to delivering affordable, effective medicines to Australians. “I have heard from people who live with this chronic skin condition and I know how painful and debilitating it can be. “This listing of aZematop will give more than one hundred thousand Australians access to an affordable treatment on the PBS. “From October, thousands of Australians with severe asthma or hives can also benefit from a new pre-filled pen form of Omlyclo on the PBS, dramatically reducing the cost.” Minister: The Hon Mark Butler MP Tags: Medicines

title: PBS listing delivers new breast cancer treatment option for Australian women
text: Media event date: 17 September 2026 Date published: 17 September 2026 Media type: Media release Audience: General public The Albanese Government is continuing to deliver cheaper medicines with thousands of women expected to benefit from expanded access to a treatment on the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS). From 1 October 2026, Triptorelin 3.75mg (Diphereline®) will become available on the PBS for the treatment[GA1] of a range of women’s health conditions, including breast cancer, endometriosis and uterine fibrosis. The expanded PBS listing of Triptorelin will provide certainty for thousands of women who have been unsure of their treatment options with the uncertainty around the listing of Zoladex 3.6mg Implant, which is currently scheduled to be delisted from the PBS from 1 November 2026 at the request of its pharmaceutical sponsor. At a special meeting in July 2026, the Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee recommended an expanded (unrestricted benefit) PBS listing for Triptorelin, to provide an alternative treatment for women In 2025, around 13,580 Australians accessed Zoladex 3.6mg Implant or a comparable treatment on the PBS. The expanded PBS listing means Triptorelin will be available as an alternative monthly treatment at PBS prices. Without PBS subsidy, patients could pay more than $1,370 per script. Now it will cost no more than $25 per script. Quotes attributable to Minister Butler: “Our government is committed to better health care for Australian women. “We know thousands of women were concerned about the prospect of losing access to the particular Zoladex treatment which is why our government has taken action to find an alternative treatment for women. “This expanded treatment option will provide certainty to women and ensure they can continue to access a monthly treatment option at an affordable price.” Quotes attributable to Assistant Minister White: “We understand how important it is to have certainty when it comes to your health and women have been concerned about the changes to Zoladex and what that could mean for their treatment. “Women should be able to access the medicines they need without cost being a barrier, particularly when they are managing conditions like breast cancer and endometriosis. “Women’s health is a priority for our government, and we’ll continue to make sure women have access to affordable treatment, more choice and better care." Quotes attributable to Breast Cancer Network Australia Director Policy, Vicki Durston: "Today’s announcement that there will be a monthly alternative, triptorelin (3.75mg), available on the PBS from 1 October 2026, provides welcome relief to women and restores their trust that a safe and effective drug is available come 1 October. “We acknowledge the work of PBAC, the Department of Health, Disability and Ageing, Ipsen, Minister Butler and his office, who heard the impact directly from Breast Cancer Network Australia's consumers and clinicians and responded to this critical issue. “We welcome the PBS listing of triptorelin and this listing provides much-needed certainty. Women should never be left asking whether a medicine they depend on will still be there whilst they need it." Minister: The Hon Mark Butler MP The Hon Rebecca White MP Tags: Cancer Women's health

title: Press conference with Minister Butler, Canberra – 17 September 2026
text: Media event date: 17 September 2026 Date published: 17 September 2026 Media type: Media release Audience: General public MARK BUTLER, MINISTER FOR HEALTH AND AGEING, MINISTER FOR DISABILITY AND THE NDIS: Thanks very much for coming out this morning. We have a very exciting important announcement around breast cancer treatment. I’m delighted to be joined by Vicki Durston, the Head of Policy and Advocacy for the Breast Cancer Network of Australia, the key peak patient organisation for Australians living with breast cancer. We’re also joined by Jenny from Cancer Nurses, who is a nurse practitioner working in breast oncology, and Katie, is a patient living with metastatic breast cancer who will talk about her personal experience here, and I really want to thank all three for coming along today. As Australians know so well, breast cancer is the most common form of cancer experienced by Australian women, and although Australia has some of the best survival rates in the world, even breast cancer survivors often need to continue with treatment for years after their primary treatment to deal with the consequences of their cancer and their cancer treatment, but also to suppress certain hormones that will drive cancer cells and raise the risk of a relapsed or reoccurrence. For many, many years now, thousands of Australian women who have survived breast cancer have relied upon a particular hormone suppressant, or GnRH agonist called Zoladex, sponsored by AstraZeneca. This is a monthly injection that around 13,500 women taken every month, often for years to reduce that risk of reoccurrence, and to give them confidence that they are going to be able to continue on with life. AstraZeneca, the sponsor of that company, made an announcement some months ago that they intended to withdraw Zoladex from the PBC for this particular dose, and that has, I’m sure Vicki and Jenny and particularly Katie will outline, caused enormous anxiety, enormous anxiety among many thousands of Australian women. Over the last few months, we’ve been working together to find a solution to this. The Breast Cancer Network, I have to express my enormous gratitude, pulled together a roundtable. We’ve been working together to do what we can to ensure security and affordability of an alternative treatment. We scanned the rest of the world and found there is an equivalent treatment called Triptorelin sponsored by a drug company called Ipsom. We invited that company to make an application to Australia, to our Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee, expedited that process, and are able to announce today that this equivalent treatment, Triptorelin, will be available on the PBS from 1 October, ensuring that there is no gap in this incredibly important hormone suppressant for Australian women. Without PBS listing, it could be available on the private market, but it would cost about $1,380 per script. It will now be available at affordable PBS prices. I really want to thank Ipsen, the sponsor company, for agreeing to act so quickly and bringing their drug to the Australian PBS market. We know how important the PBS is for Australian patients. It obviously gives them access to the world’s best treatments at affordable prices, but it also gives them the security that that drug will be available for them when they need it. I’m going to hand over now to Vicki to talk about this from the perspective of BCNA, and then to Jenny and then to Katie, and then happy to take questions. VICKI DURSTON, BREAST CANCER NETWORK AUSTRALIA, DIRECTOR OF POLICY AND ADVOCACY: Thanks, Minister. Today's PBS listing of monthly Triptorelin is incredibly important, as mentioned by the Minister, for women affected by breast cancer. And this is certainly an important day in what has been a confusing and very uncertain period for the last four months. And I think it's important to understand why. For women who require ovarian suppression, it is a critical part of their breast cancer treatment. Put really simply, some breast cancers are fuelled by oestrogen. Ovarian suppression switches off a major source of that fuel. It is used to reduce the risk of cancer returning, as the Minister mentioned, to help control metastatic breast cancer and prolong life, and for some younger women to help protect ovarian function and preserve the possibility of having children in the future. This is a cancer treatment. It's about controlling disease, protecting life and preserving choices for the future. a treatment made available and has been used for 30 years. And that's why when AstraZeneca announced that monthly Zoladex would be discontinued in Australia, the concern was very real. And at that point, there was no confirmed monthly alternative on the PBS. So imagine, you're a woman relying on this treatment, you're thinking, what happens to my treatment now? Will my cancer progress? Will my cancer start growing? No woman should be left fearing what happens next. We also saw women making incredibly different, difficult decisions about their bodies and their futures because they needed certainty. Some chose to have their ovaries surgically removed, like Katie here today, and she'll talk more about this. And I think that tells you just how significant this became. And trust was tested. So our job at Breast Cancer Network Australia was to listen to what women were telling us, bring those experiences together with the clinical evidence and work constructively with government to really look to find a solution. Our ask was very clear. Women needed a funded monthly alternative before Zoladex was withdrawn, come 1 November. I want to acknowledge all the courageous women and advocates who came forward. We want to acknowledge Minister Butler and the Assistant Health Minister White, the team from the Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee and the Department of Health led by Daniel, who really stepped up, and really heard the impact directly from those of lived experience, clinicians and Breast Cancer Network Australia, who responded to this critical issue. And I want to acknowledge Ipsen. When an alternative was needed, Ipsen stepped forward with Triptorelin and established safe and effective treatment equivalently used internationally for decades, working at pace with government through the processes required to make it available to Australian women come 1 October. And that brings us to today. Women now have what they are needed through this process, continuity treatment, certainty and choice. There still may be many questions and Breast Cancer Network Australia will continue to be here to support and answer all those questions as we transition through. But today we can finally say to women, there is a funded monthly treatment option for those who need it. And after the uncertainty of the past few months, that is an incredibly important outcome. Thank you. JENNY GILCHRIST, NURSE PRACTITIONER, CANCER NURSES SOCIETY OF AUSTRALIA: Minister Butler, thank you for the opportunity to speak today. As a breast oncology clinician, every day I see how important ovarian suppression is for young women with cancer. For women undergoing chemotherapy, it can help protect ovarian function and preserve the possibility of future fertility. In hormone receptor positive breast cancer, ovarian suppression is also a critical part of anti-cancer treatment. And the impact extends beyond breast cancer, with these medications also used by women with other cancers and conditions such as endometriosis. When AstraZeneca made the commercial decision to remove the monthly Zoladex formulation from the Australian market, it threw many women, and quite frankly many of us caring for them, into disarray. Women already dealing with the enormous uncertainty of a cancer diagnosis were suddenly asking whether they would still have access to a treatment that they relied on, whether they would need to change their treatment or even whether they should consider having their ovaries surgically removed. That is an extraordinary burden to place on women who already have enough to deal with. And that is why the PBS listing of Triptorelin is so important. Triptorelin is not a new or experimental treatment, and importantly, the evidence is for Triptorelin itself. It was the ovarian suppression therapy used in the landmark trials which helped establish ovarian suppression as a part of standard cancer treatment for premenopausal women with hormone receptor positive breast cancer. We also have robust randomised trial data showing that Triptorelin, given throughout chemotherapy significantly reduces the risk of chemotherapy-induced early menopause and improves the likelihood of ovarian function recovery after treatment. Triptorelin is not an unknown substitution. It has its own strong evidence base, has been used in women with breast cancer internationally for many, years, and as clinicians, we can have real confidence prescribing it. The PBS listing now means that we have clear evidence-based treatment pathway moving forward. Women going through cancer treatment should be able to focus on getting well, not on whether an essential medicine will be suddenly just taken off the market because of a commercial decision. For our patients, having that certainty matters enormously. KATIE-MARIE THORPE, PATIENT: Thanks, Jenny. Today’s announcement that Triptorelin will be available on the PBS is a very welcome step forward after months and months of uncertainty for women in the breast cancer, endometriosis and wider women’s health communities who rely on ovarian suppression as part of their treatment. I just want to paint a picture of what the past few months have looked like for those of us who may not have been living it. In June this year, thousands of women woke up to the headline saying that Zoladex 3.6 milligrams would be delisted from the PBS and the Australian market with no viable alternative. There had been no warning from our oncologists or treating teams, no clear official communication telling us what would happen next, we simply woke up to a headline, read the news, and if you were like me, thought, hang on, that’s my medication keeping me alive. Zoladex was not just another prescription, it was part of the treatment to keep my advanced breast cancer from spreading. A metastatic diagnosis guarantees a life full of hard uncertainties, but whether I can access the treatment that my oncologist prescribes should never be one of them. That uncertainty became part of that catalyst for a decision that I cannot undo, I chose to have my ovaries removed. That meant surgery, weeks of recovery and permanently entering surgical menopause at 34 years of age. It also meant having to confront finally and irreversibly that I would never carry a child. It may sound like an extreme reaction, but I was not the only woman having that conversation. Women right around Australia were sitting in specialist rooms discussing permanent surgery options because there was no certainty about what ovarian suppressing treatment would be available to them in the months ahead. Nobody should be making irreversible decisions about their body because they are afraid a medicine might disappear. And that is why today matters. Today gives women clarity, certainty and choice. I want to thank the Minister, when I sat with him last month and spoke about the ripple that this had caused in our community and the position that women had been placed in, he listened. To see the action follow so quickly really matters to us. It shows strong leadership and it shows what can happen when patients are heard and their experiences are taken seriously. We need a healthcare system that understands the people it exists to support. Commercial decisions will happen and governments may not always be able to prevent them, but our health system can decide what happens next. Patients should not be the ones left to carry the burden while decisions around them are made. I want to thank Ipsen for stepping up and providing Triptorelin as another option when there was no certainty about a suitable ovarian suppressing treatment, and I want to acknowledge Breast Cancer Network Australia for the tireless and fearless advocacy throughout this. They’ve kept pushing for women to have safe, accessible treatment at an incredibly vulnerable point in their lives, and this is why we have this positive outcome today. Thank you also to the advocacy groups, clinicians, advocates and women who kept asking questions and refusing to let this issue disappear. I truly believe the best advocacy is not the kind that opens the door for one person, it is the kind that holds the door open for everyone coming in behind them. Somewhere in Australia, there will be a woman sitting in an oncology room in the months or years ahead, hearing that she needs ovarian suppression as part of her cancer treatment. She may already be frightened, I can definitely guarantee she’ll be frightened, she may be thinking about reoccurrence, fertility, side effects, family, work, all the other things, or whether the protocol in front of her is going to keep her alive. Because of today’s announcement, at least one of those fears will be removed. She will have options and the chance to choose what is right for her body with her doctor. Living with cancer will always come with things that we cannot control. But today, women have been given some of that control back. And for thousands of women in our community, that means so much more than just another medicine being listed on the PBS. Thank you. BUTLER : Thank you, Katie, and Jenny and Vicki, but Katie particularly for telling your personal story, which you've done a number of times and is a hard thing for you to do, I'm sure, but is a really powerful motivation for government and others to act. Happy to take questions on this. JOURNALIST : Minister, there have been a few cases of pharmaceutical companies withdrawing really important drugs like Zoladex. What more can be done to safeguard the Australian market from things like this happening again? BUTLER : You're right. We've seen a number this year. This has been a very high-profile example of that, but you'll remember there are a couple of incredibly important multiple sclerosis, or MS, drugs that were proposed for withdrawal on the PBS. Again, we ensured that there was an expedited process through the Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee to forestall that and to keep those drugs on the PBS. There's more work happening now about MS treatments over the course of the rest of this year. And I think what both of these cases demonstrate is the need at a time when the pharmaceutical industry globally has been really, frankly, upended to a degree by US Administration policy changes, that we are going to have to remain agile. We need to put in place some policy responses to ensure we protect the PBS and those core missions of the PBS, to ensure that Australians have access to the world's best medicines and they are priced affordably through PBS arrangements. But from time to time, I suspect right now, we're going to have to respond to these commercial decisions that Katie and Vicki and Jenny talked about being taken by sponsors, not here in Australia, but frankly in the global headquarters in Europe or Japan or the US. We're going to have to respond in an agile way, and I'm really, really proud of the fact that in partnership with the patient community, our department and the Pharmaceutical Benefits Advisory Committee have acted very, very quickly in scanning the global market, then inviting Ipsen, and I thank them again for being willing to participate in this process. JOURNALIST : In withdrawing their drugs, pharmaceutical companies have been critical that the government has yet to fully respond to the recommendations from the HTA review. How is that progressing? BUTLER : We do have to take that process forward. I announced last September a number of priority actions which are underway, particularly around a couple of the core criticisms that pharmaceutical companies make of the PBS guidelines, particularly the selection of comparator medicines when they're applying for listing, the discount rate, things like that are already underway. But we also recognise there’s a bigger piece of work for us to do as government, in partnership with the pharmaceutical industry, but also with patient groups like BCNA to set up the PBS for the future. We were intending to do that anyway, even before the US administration policy changes. That's added a particular element to it, or dynamic to it as well, and we'll be doing that as part of the renegotiation of our strategic agreements with Medicines Australia that is in the process of kicking off as we speak. JOURNALIST : In terms of the AstraZeneca access program that was going to happen for Zoladex, have you spoken to them? Do you anticipate that they'll now fully withdraw Zoladex and not run this access program, given an equivalent is about to hit the market? BUTLER : That's really a matter for AstraZeneca. There had been a number of pieces of coverage, I think including through you, about whether that program was going to be ongoing or for a fixed period. And I think that just goes to reflect the messages you've heard there about the uncertainty that this sponsor announcement had for women undertaking this treatment. At the end of the day, listing on the PBS is that security, that certainty, as well as that affordability. And so even if there were a private market arrangement, our view as government, and I think the view of BCNA and the community was, we needed a treatment on the PBS because that is the core guarantee of security, certainty and affordability. JOURNALIST : What, if any, costs will there be to the budget? Or is it just offset by Zoladex? BUTLER : Yeah, we think this broadly will be neutral because this is really a substitution of a treatment, like for like. As Vicki and Jenny said, this is regarded as an equivalent treatment It's a monthly injection that will be received in the same way by patients through their treating clinicians, nurse practitioners or doctors, and effectively for the government should be budget neutral. JOURNALIST : Minister, you said that without a PBS listing that Triptorelin would cost $1,380 per script. Can you tell patients what sort of range they should be expecting to pay now? I know you said affordable, but what should they be looking at? BUTLER : For a general patient that will be $25 a script, which would be what they would be paying now. For concessional patients that would be $7.70 a script. Standard PBS prices. JOURNALIST : Can I maybe just ask one for Vicki? BUTLER : Yeah, please. JOURNALIST : I know it's early days, but I was just interested in what the response has been so far to this news from the community. DURSTON : Yeah, thank you so much for the question. And I think that certainly what we've seen is the importance of, like the Minister mentioned, we need to have an option on the PBS, and that was something that we stood firm in calling for. Today presents that opportunity for women. There's still a lot of questions that obviously women want to know, and that's why Breast Cancer Network Australia will be ensuring that we can answer those questions. Certainly, what we're hearing is that women want options and choices. So what this demonstrated is when a well-established drug that's on the PBS is removed from the PBS and with no other option, that created the fear and uncertainty. So today is a welcomed announcement. And certainly, it is something though, that will remain on our agenda through advocacy. And certainly, we'll be working with our global partners and obviously advocates around the country to continue to monitor and also work with government to ensure that those, when this happens, and if this happens again, that we're ready and that we're able to respond accordingly. Thanks. JOURNALIST : On the move to ditch the proposed $5,000 veterans’ allied health cap, do you regret initially pursuing this? BUTLER : Without going back over the reasons for the design that we had in this budget measure, let me say a couple of things. As the son of a Vietnam veteran and the grandson of two World War Two veterans and veterans further back in other conflicts Australia has been involved in, I understand very, very intimately the importance of strong veteran health services. What the government has been particularly focused on and we will continue to do is to lift the rebates or the prices paid for allied health services for veterans. Because what we were finding is that veterans were having difficulty getting access to allied health services because the price being paid through the veterans’ program was lower than allied health practitioners or allied health professionals were able to receive through other social programs. This is often a slightly overlooked element of the budget decision, but we're going to maintain that so that veterans have better access. But we've heard the message from the veterans’ community. We understand that this does not have a pathway through the Senate, and so we won't be proceeding with the changes to the cap arrangement, the existing cap arrangements that require veterans to go back to their GP after 12 visits and substituting that with the $5,000 review arrangement. Not going to go into the whys and wherefores of that. We've heard the message from the veterans’ community and we won't be proceeding with that. We want to focus today on legislation that is in the Senate that will directly implement 20 additional recommendations of the Royal Commission into Veteran Suicide and support the further implementation of another 20. This is the business now that we want the Senate to get on with over the course of today. JOURNALIST : Is this is a misstep from the government to try and do this, given the veteran community was already sounding the alarm before the budget? BUTLER : We came to this position, I know the Minister came to this position, trying to improve access to veterans’ allied health. As I said, increasing that price paid for allied health services through the veterans’ program, critically important. I don't want to go back over the reasons why the review arrangements were being proposed to change from 12 visits to $5000. We’ve heard the message from the veterans’ community, heard the message from the Senate about that, and we won't be proceeding with that. We think it's so important that we get on with the business with implementing other recommendations of the Royal Commission into Veteran Suicide, and that business is before the Senate today. JOURNALIST : It was a measure of the budget designed to save the government money. Is there other measures now being proposed to make up for the shortfall? BUTLER : Our focus today is on the announcement we've made this morning and on the really important legislation before the Senate. JOURNALIST : Speaking on pathways through the Senate, the Greens have said you need to fix the private health insurance rebate legislation. Are you in discussions with them? Are you open to amending the legislation in order to get it through? BUTLER : The legislation has passed the House. It then moves to the Senate at some time, probably in October or November. Preferably October, given the need for us to start the annual premium round. There's a Senate inquiry underway that's not due to report until 8 October. We're monitoring the evidence before that, the submissions to that, and probably we intend to wait until the report is delivered on 8 October. And then, of course, we'll have to have discussions with Senate parties. JOURNALIST : What about carving out pensioners? Are you open to that? BUTLER : Look, I don't want to pre-empt what the report may deliver in terms of its findings and recommendations, but we're taking this seriously as we do all Senate inquiries, and recognise that once that's been delivered, we'll sit down with Senate parties, including the Greens, whom you mentioned, and talk about this reform. JOURNALIST : What will the hit to the budget be with this backflip? BUTLER : We'll update that in the usual way. Are you talking about veterans’ health services? JOURNALIST : Yeah, sorry. BUTLER : We'll update that in the usual way through the MYEFO process. Thanks, everyone. Minister: The Hon Mark Butler MP Tags: Medicines

title: Australian Government delivers major mental health boost for young people in Wagga Wagga
text: Media event date: 17 September 2026 Date published: 17 September 2026 Media type: Media release Audience: General public The Albanese Labor Government is boosting funding for headspace Wagga Wagga, expanding access to free mental health care for young people across the Riverina. Over the next 12 months, headspace Wagga Wagga will transition to headspace Plus, an enhanced model of care designed to support young people experiencing more severe and complex mental health challenges. The investment builds on the Government’s strong record of supporting local young people through the centre, delivering more than 4,300 free appointments to over 1,100 locals in the last year alone. Through the expansion, headspace Wagga Wagga will increase its specialist workforce and service capacity, enabling more young people to access more care, closer to home. The headspace Plus model brings together psychologists, social workers, counsellors and peer workers to provide coordinated, multidisciplinary support for young people with more complex needs, while retaining the accessible and youth-friendly approach that headspace is known for. Wagga Wagga will be among the first 10 centres nationally to deliver the headspace Plus model. Nationally, headspace provides free mental health support for young people aged 12 to 25 experiencing, or at risk of, mental ill-health, as well as assistance with physical and sexual health, alcohol and other drug issues, and work and study challenges. Over the past year, the Albanese Labor Government has invested more than $211.5 million to establish 56 new headspace services across Australia, including the transition of 30 centres to headspace Plus. For young people who prefer online support, eheadspace is available at: www.headspace.org.au or by phoning 1800 650 890. Quotes attributable to Assistant Minister McBride: “Young people in regional Australia deserve access to the mental health care they need, close to home. “Two decades ago, one in five young people experienced mental health challenges. Today, it's two in five. The challenge has grown, and so must we. “By doubling funding for headspace Wagga Wagga and upgrading the service to headspace Plus, we're making sure more young people can access coordinated, specialised support sooner. “This is about meeting locals where they are with the help they need.” Minister: The Hon Emma McBride MP Tags: Mental health and suicide prevention

title: New CEO for the Organ and Tissue Authority
text: Media event date: 17 September 2026 Date published: 17 September 2026 Media type: Media release Audience: General public The Albanese Government has appointed Ms Helen Grinbergs as the Chief Executive Officer of the Organ and Tissue Authority (OTA) for a five-year term from 1 October 2026. Ms Grinbergs brings extensive experience to the position, having held a range of high-profile roles in aged care, and national and international health. Most recently, she led the work to establish the Australian Centre for Disease Control and was instrumental in leading work to support aged care during the pandemic. The OTA leads the national DonateLife program which has helped more than 20,000 Australians to receive a lifesaving or life-changing organ transplant since 2009. While 4 in 5 Australians aged 16+ support organ and tissue donation – only 1 in 3 are registered to donate. There are currently around 1,800 people on organ waitlists who need Australia’s help. Registering as an organ donor only takes one minute. Australians are encouraged to Join the register | DonateLife and talk to their family about their decision. Ms Grinbergs replaces Ms Lucinda Barry AM who has served as Chief Executive Officer of the OTA since 2017. Ms Barry’s contributions were recognised in 2023 when she was appointed a Member of the Order of Australia. The Albanese Government thanks Ms Barry for her leadership and the significant contribution she made to give more Australians a second chance at life. Quotes attributable to Assistant Minister White: “I thank Ms Barry for her service and incredible contribution to the Australian community over the past decade as Chief Executive Officer of the Organ and Tissue Authority. “I welcome Ms Grinbergs to the role and look forward to working with her to further improve organ and tissue donation and transplantation outcomes for Australians. “Organ and tissue donation is an incredible act of generosity that can change someone’s life and the lives of the people that love them. "I encourage every Australian to talk to their families about donation and register as a donor.” Minister: The Hon Rebecca White MP Tags: Organ and tissue donation

title: Better transparency and choice in health care
text: Media event date: 16 September 2026 Date published: 16 September 2026 Media type: Media release Audience: General public The Australian Government has passed legislation to help Australians find the best value when they need specialist medical advice and treatment, fixing the failed Medical Costs Finder. The Morrison Government spent $24 million setting up the Medical Costs Finder website, which it claimed would use Medicare data to display the cost of common medical services, alongside the fees that individual specialists voluntarily shared to the website. By the end of 2022, only 6 individual doctors had chosen to voluntarily display their fee information – and now 4 years later that has only risen to 106 doctors, out of around 6,300 eligible specialists. To improve transparency and take the guess work out of health care, the Health Legislation Amendment (Improving Choice and Transparency for Private Health Consumers) Bill 2026 will allow the government to publish the fees of individual specialists for common medical services and out-of-pocket costs. In addition, this legislation also outlaws the practice known as ‘product phoenixing’, where private health insurers close a product and re-open a similar one at a higher price, or reduce its value. This legislation requires insurers to seek Ministerial approval for premiums for new products and if making certain changes that reduce the cover or value of existing products. Quotes attributable to Minister Butler: “This legislation amendment delivers on our election commitment to Australians. “It addresses long-standing information gaps that contribute to cost uncertainty, and it gives Australians better transparency and choice with their health care. “We know an increasing number of Australians have not been taking up referrals from their GP to see a specialist due to concern about cost, but this legislation will deliver clarity about costs and more choice in their health care. “The legislation also provides wider scrutiny of premiums to ensure Australians get fair premiums and better value.” Minister: The Hon Mark Butler MP Tags: Medicare Private health insurance

title: Australian Government investment to bring international clinical trial access to Australia, for childhood cancer
text: Media event date: 12 September 2026 Date published: 12 September 2026 Media type: Media release Audience: General public The Australian Government is delivering the first investment under the $300 million MRFF Australian Cancer Research Program (ACRP), to bring international CAR-T clinical trials to Australia for children and young people. The Government is committing $5 million in grant funding over 5 years from 2027-28 to support Australian participation in the LifeArc Worldwide CAR-T Pathfinder Trial and Paediatric Cell Therapy Accelerator. The ACRP is a landmark $300 million, 10-year MRFF investment to strengthen and coordinate cancer research nationally and includes the Childhood, Adolescent and Young Adult (CAYA) Cancer Mission. This will mark a significant first for Australia, helping to bring international CAR-T clinical trial capability closer to home for children and young people. The grant opportunity responds to priorities in Cancer Australia's Childhood, Adolescent and Young Adult Cancer Roadmap, released earlier this year as a national framework to improve outcomes and experiences for Australians aged up to 24 years affected by cancer. The MRFF ACRP grant opportunity is forecast to open in June 2027. Further research priorities and funding intentions will be announced in the coming months. Quotes attributable to the Minister for Health and Ageing, the Hon Mark Butler MP: "Earlier this year, we announced the Australian Cancer Research Program, a landmark $300 million investment under the Medical Research Future Fund to drive a stronger, more coordinated national effort in cancer research. "Now, we are taking an important first step in delivering that commitment through the first grant opportunity under the Childhood, Adolescent and Young Adult Cancer Mission. "It will help bring world-class international CAR-T clinical trials closer to home for Australian children and young people with cancer. "More families may be able to access promising new therapies in Australia, rather than facing the significant financial and emotional burden of travelling overseas for treatment." Quotes attributable to Professor Dorothy Keefe PSM, Chief Executive Officer, Cancer Australia: "Cancer Australia welcomes this important first investment under the Childhood, Adolescent and Young Adult Cancer Mission." "The Childhood, Adolescent and Young Adult Cancer Roadmap provides national direction for improving outcomes and experiences, and this announcement demonstrates early progress in implementing its priorities." "Together, we have an opportunity to build a more connected national childhood and young adult cancer system and deliver lasting improvements in care, research and outcomes." Quotes attributable to Professor Brendan Murphy AC, Chair of Children’s Cancer CoLab: “It is very encouraging to see the Australian Government investing in new treatment options for children and young people with cancer. "This important and timely investment through the Childhood, Adolescent and Young Adult Cancer Mission, building on the Optimal Care Pathway in development, provides exciting opportunities to facilitate access to, and further local development of, novel therapies and best practice models of care.” Quotes attributable to Owen Finegan, CEO, The Kids’ Cancer Project “Today’s announcement is an important reminder that improving outcomes for children and young people with cancer requires a genuinely collaborative, whole-of-sector approach. Government, Cancer Australia, like-minded charities, clinicians, researchers, allied health professionals, advocates and people with lived experience all bring different strengths, perspectives and expertise to the table. “The Roadmap and the Childhood, Adolescent and Young Adults Cancer Mission provide a significant opportunity to bring those strengths together around a shared national purpose that will turn ambition into meaningful action.” Minister: The Hon Mark Butler MP Tags: Cancer

title: New PBS listing for Australians living with motor neurone disease
text: Media event date: 11 September 2026 Date published: 11 September 2026 Media type: Media release Audience: General public Australians living with a type of Motor Neurone Disease (MND) will have access to a new cheaper treatment through the Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme (PBS). From October 1, Tofersen (Qalsody®) will be listed for the first time for the treatment of MND patients with a form of Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Around 2,800 Australians are estimated to be living with motor neurone disease and ALS is a particular disease accounting for up to 90% of MND cases. ALS is a progressive neurological condition that damages the nerve cells that control muscle movement. Over time, this can affect a person’s ability to move, speak, swallow and breathe, leading to increasing disability and loss of independence. Qalsody is a targeted treatment for patients with a rare genetic form of ALS. It works by reducing the production of SOD1 protein and offers a new treatment option for patients with limited existing therapies. The treatment may slow disease progression and help patients maintain function for longer. Around 70 Australians are expected to benefit from this listing each year. Without PBS subsidy, it would cost patients up to $28,600 per script. This is the second treatment for MND listed on the PBS under the Albanese Government, on top of the establishment of the Neale Daniher National MND Clinical Network, giving more people with MND access to treatment trials. PBS listing means eligible patients will pay a maximum of $25 per script, or just $7.70 with a concession card. Quotes attributable to Minister Butler: “MND is a heartbreaking insidious disease that Australians are all too familiar with. “The listing of Qalsody for ALS on the PBS is a gamechanger for Australian patients. “With every investment the Albanese Government makes in new research and treatments for MND, we hope to honour the great legacy of Neale Daniher. “That is why our Government recently committed $40.1 million to establish the Neale Daniher MND Clinical Network – to strengthen our efforts to find new therapies and improve quality of life for people living with MND. "And now the new listing of Qalsody on the PBS for patients with ALS, is also ensuring Neale’s extraordinary legacy will continue to make a difference in the lives of Australians living with MND.” Minister: The Hon Mark Butler MP Tags: Chronic conditions

title: Australian Government set to improve access to affordable contraception across Australia
text: Media event date: 11 September 2026 Date published: 11 September 2026 Media type: Media release Audience: General public Women across Australia will soon have more choice and better access to long-acting reversible contraception, with leading centres set to provide the gold standard in women’s contraceptive care across the country. The Albanese Government has invested $25 million to establish eight LARC Centres of Excellence to make it easier for women to access long-acting contraception including IUDS and contraceptive implants. As part of the program, women can receive free advice from skilled providers about their contraceptive options, as well as the insertion and removal of IUDS and birth control implants. Long-acting reversible contraceptives are among the most effective forms of contraception available, with effectiveness rates of more than 99 per cent. In addition to preventing unintended pregnancy, some can also help manage heavy menstrual bleeding, period pain and conditions such as endometriosis. Outreach services will support women in regional, rural and remote communities by bringing contraceptive services and training opportunities closer to where people live and work. The centres will be operated by the providers from 31 October: Sexual Health and Family Planning ACT Family Planning Welfare Association of NT Family Planning Australia, NSW True Relationships and Reproductive Health, Qld Family Planning Tasmania SHINE SA Sexual Health Quarters, WA Sexual Health Victoria. The LARC Centres of Excellence are part of the Albanese Government’s landmark nearly $800 million Women's Health Package that is continuing to deliver on its promise of more choice, lower costs and better care for women. Quotes attributable to Assistant Minister White: "We want every Australian woman to know their health is a priority of the Albanese Government and we want women to be able to choose the contraception that works best for them, not simply the option that is easiest to access or the one they can afford. “Long-acting contraceptives are safe, highly effective and can be life changing for some women, but we know they haven’t always been easy to access. “With all eight centres now a step closer to opening their doors, more women will be able to access the information, support and care they need to make the choice that is right for them. “A really important part of these centres is training more doctors, nurses and health professionals, so women can have these conversations and access the care they need closer to home." title: Strengthening suicide prevention support for all Australians
text: Media event date: 10 September 2026 Date published: 10 September 2026 Media type: Media release Audience: General public On World Suicide Prevention Day, the Albanese Labor Government will provide an additional $82.9 million to leading national suicide prevention services and illuminate Australian Parliament House in recognition of all those affected by suicide. Suicide prevention remains a key priority for the Albanese Labor Government. Tragically, more than 3,000 Australians lose their lives to suicide each year, leaving families, friends and communities to carry the profound and lasting impact of that loss. To help reduce suicide and suicidal distress, the Government will deliver an additional $82.9 million through the National Suicide Prevention Leadership and Support Program (NSPLSP), supporting 36 organisations delivering evidence-based suicide prevention initiatives across the country. The NSPLSP strengthens prevention, early intervention and postvention support, with a particular focus on groups disproportionately impacted by suicide, including men, First Nations peoples, LGBTQIA+ Australians, people living in regional and remote areas, veterans and young people. Through the program, organisations including Suicide Prevention Australia, R U OK? and MATES in Construction will deliver vital programs that help save lives, strengthen communities and support people when they need it most. The program also supports Mental Health First Aid Australia, which has trained more than 1.6 million Australians to recognise the signs of mental ill-health and provide evidence-based support to people experiencing mental health challenges or suicidal distress. While progress is being made, one life lost to suicide is one too many. This year's World Suicide Prevention Day theme, Change the Narrative , highlights the importance of reducing stigma, encouraging open conversations and making sure people know that help is available. At dusk on World Suicide Prevention Day and R U OK?Day, Australian Parliament House will be illuminated in yellow and orange to honour those lost to suicide, recognise those impacted and encourage Australians to check in with one another. This will be the first time Parliament House has been illuminated to mark World Suicide Prevention Day. Making sure Australians can access support when they need it is central to the Australian Government's approach to mental health and suicide prevention. The Government has invested $1.1 billion to expand free mental health services across the country, including growing the national network of Medicare Mental Health Centres to 92 locations. There are currently 57 Medicare Mental Health Centres operating across Australia, providing free, walk-in mental health care without the need for an appointment or referral. The Government has also launched Medicare Mental health Check In, Australia’s first digital mental health service – making sure Australians can access free, expert advice wherever they are. If you are or someone you know is seeking support or information, you can call Medicare Mental Health on 1800 595 212 or visit www.medicarementalhealth.gov.au People seeking support for suicidal ideation are encouraged to call Lifeline, Beyond Blue, 13YARN or visit a Medicare Mental Health Centre. Quotes attributed to Minister Butler: “ Every day in Australia, a devastating nine people die by suicide and more than 150 attempt to take their own life, but it doesn’t have to be this way. “The Albanese Government is investing almost $83 million to deliver evidence-based suicide prevention programs right across the country, to help reduce suicide and suicidal distress.” Quotes attributed to Assistant Minister McBride: "Every life lost to suicide is a tragedy, and every death leaves a profound and lasting impact on families, friends and communities. "That's why the Albanese Labor Government is investing an additional $82.9 million in leading suicide prevention organisations, supporting the services that save lives and help Australians through their darkest moments. "We know these services save lives, but suicide prevention doesn't just happen in clinics or support services. It can start with a simple conversation, checking in on a friend, family member or colleague, not only today on World Suicide Prevention Day, but every day. "On World Suicide Prevention Day, we remember those we have lost, support those affected, and renew our commitment to making sure everyone gets they need when they need it." title: Protecting older Australians in residential aged care
text: Media event date: 10 September 2026 Date published: 10 September 2026 Media type: Media release Audience: General public The Albanese Government is continuing to strengthen protections for older Australians in residential aged care through changes that respond to feedback from residents, their families, carers, advocates and providers. Labor will amend the Aged Care Rules 2025 to protect aged care residents from being charged a Higher Everyday Living Fee (HELF) for services they were previously receiving at no extra cost. Government guidance has made it clear that it is unreasonable for providers to charge a HELF for services an older Australian in residential aged care had previously received at no additional cost prior to 1 November 2025. After instances of some providers doing the wrong thing and taking advantage of older Australians and their families, we’re now moving to ensure this expectation is codified in law to ensure people can continue to receive the safe, dignified and high-quality aged care they deserve, wherever they live. As part of our ongoing work to strengthen and monitor the system, we found that some providers were asking existing residents to pay for continued access to services previously provided at no extra cost. This was in stark contrast to the advice from Government and residents in some cases also faced uncertainty about whether services would continue if they did not agree to pay. Under the changes announced today, residential aged care providers will not be able to charge residents a HELF for services they were receiving as part of their care arrangements before 1 November 2025. The legislative changes will provide certainty for residents, their families and carers, and providers by clarifying how the fee applies to people who were already living in residential aged care before 1 November 2025. This announcement builds on the package of consumer protections Labor announced earlier this year, which included empowering the Aged Care Quality and Safety Commission to order refunds when providers are found to be out of line with their obligations under law. The Government will continue to update guidance in relation to HELF when necessary to ensure the standards meet community expectations as the aged care reforms mature. Quotes attributable to the Minister for Aged Care and Seniors, Sam Rae MP: “We’ve always said it was unreasonable for providers to start charging older Australians for services they previously received at no cost. We’ve listened to older people and we are acting now to make the rules clear and strengthen protections for older Australians. “We've been very clear, the Higher Everyday Living Fee is for optional, additional services people choose to receive, not services that were already part of their everyday care. – it’s common sense that services a provider was already delivering, continue to be provided at no additional cost." title: More choice, lower costs for one million women
text: Media event date: 7 September 2026 Date published: 7 September 2026 Media type: Media release Audience: General public More than one million Australian women have accessed cheaper medicines for contraception, endometriosis and menopause thanks to the Australian Government’s landmark nearly $800 million Women’s Health Package. The new figures released during Women’s Health Week, shows the Australian Government is continuing to deliver on its promise of more choice, lower costs and better care for Australian women and girls. Since March 2025, more than one million women have filled over four million cheaper prescriptions for oral contraceptives, menopausal hormone therapies, and endometriosis treatments listed on the PBS, resulting in more than $150 million in savings. The new PBS listings are giving women more affordable options at different stages of their lives. The first PBS listing for new contraceptive pills in more than 30 years and two more forms of contraceptives has helped more than 400,000 women save over $55 million on 1.27 million scripts, which previously could cost up to $380 a year. The first PBS listing of new menopausal hormone therapies in over 20 years has helped 520,000 women save $110 million on 3 million scripts, which previously could cost up to $670 a year. More than 11,000 women with endometriosis have accessed treatment at PBS prices, saving $11.7 million on 600,000 scripts, which previously could cost up to $2,700 a year. These medicines are now available for no more than $25 per PBS script or $7.70 for concession card holders. The Australian Government’s Women’s Health Package continues to deliver on its promise of more choice, lower costs and better care for Australian women with: All 33 Endometriosis and Pelvic Pain Clinics open across the country that now also support perimenopause and menopause care. More than 137,000 women have undergone a menopause health assessment since being covered by Medicare. Australian women are also benefitting from new Medicare items for longer consultation times and higher rebates for specialised gynaecological care. Larger Medicare payments and more bulk billing for IUDs and contraceptive implants continue to save women up to $400 in out-of-pocket costs a year, improving access. The first national awareness campaign on menopause and perimenopause to reduce stigma by normalising conversations about menopause and perimenopause. We know there is more to do to improve women's health, and our work doesn't stop here. That's why we have established a new Senate Select Committee on Women's Health to look at issues including fertility, postpartum healthcare and women’s pain. Our Ministerial Expert Panel on Women's Health is focused on where we can improve health outcomes for women, starting with cardiovascular disease. Women's Health Week provides an important opportunity to celebrate progress, raise awareness of ongoing health challenges, and ensure women have the information, support and services they need to thrive at every stage of life. Quotes attributable to Minister Gallagher: “More than one million women are now benefiting from cheaper medicines and greater choice because of the investments the Albanese Labor Government has made in women’s health. “This is what our Women’s Health Package is about, making women’s health care more affordable and accessible, while helping ease cost-of-living pressures for women and families. “Whether it’s contraception, endometriosis treatment or menopause care, women should be able to access the medicines they need without cost being a barrier.” Quotes attributable to Minister Butler: “All Australian women deserve to have their health issues taken seriously and given the priority they deserve. “Our government is doing that, delivering women more choice, lower costs and better access to services and treatments.” Quotes attributable to Assistant Minister White: "We listened to women when they told us they wanted more affordable options and greater choice and now more than one million women are benefitting from cheaper medicines. "That's more money back in women's pockets, but importantly, it's also more choice when it comes to their health and the care that's right for them. "Women's Health Week is a reminder to all women to make our health a priority. Women spend so much of their live taking care of everyone else and too often their own health ends up down the list. “So make the appointment you’ve been putting off, have that conversation about your health with a doctor or even just a friend and make time for you."
